title: Timolol Eye Drops: Systemic Beta-Blocker Effects
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Ophthalmic timolol lowers intraocular pressure but can still be absorbed systemically and cause bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, or bronchospasm. Check the cardiovascular and respiratory history, teach punctal occlusion, and report symptomatic pulse or breathing changes.
recognize: A slow pulse, dizziness, syncope, wheezing, or new dyspnea after eye-drop use may reflect systemic beta-blockade.
Risk is higher with asthma/COPD, conduction disease, or concurrent systemic beta blockers and other rate-slowing drugs.
priorities: Assess pulse, blood pressure, respiratory symptoms, and relevant cardiac history when concerns arise.
Use correct eye-drop technique and nasolacrimal occlusion when instructed to reduce systemic absorption.
Escalate wheeze, syncope, marked bradycardia, or heart-block symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend pulse, BP, respiratory symptoms, dizziness/falls, and therapeutic eye follow-up.
interventions: Avoid touching the dropper tip to the eye or lashes.
Separate different ophthalmic medications by the prescribed interval.
medicationSafety: Topical ophthalmic beta blockers are not purely local drugs.
Concurrent systemic beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker therapy can increase bradycardia/conduction risk.
teaching: After instilling the drop, gently close the eye and press the inner canthus as instructed; report breathing difficulty or fainting.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows state/facility scope; new cardiopulmonary symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming an eye drop cannot affect heart rate or lungs because it is topical.
oneLinePearl: Timolol in the eye can still behave like a beta blocker in the body.

title: Latanoprost: Pigment, Lashes, and Adherence
bottomLine: Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog used to lower intraocular pressure. It can permanently darken iris pigmentation and increase eyelash growth, while contamination or incorrect multi-drop timing can reduce treatment safety and adherence.
recognize: Expected local effects can include conjunctival redness, eyelash growth, periocular skin change, and gradual iris darkening.
Sudden severe eye pain, acute vision loss, or major inflammation is not an expected routine effect.
priorities: Verify the ordered eye and frequency.
Use clean drop technique and separate other ophthalmic medications by the prescribed interval.
Report significant ocular inflammation or abrupt vision change.
assessMonitor: Monitor adherence, eye redness/pain, vision change, and ophthalmology follow-up for intraocular pressure.
interventions: Remove contact lenses before administration when product instructions require it and replace them after the stated interval.
Avoid multiple doses to compensate for one missed dose unless specifically instructed.
medicationSafety: More frequent dosing does not improve effect and can reduce efficacy for prostaglandin analogs.
Iris color change may be permanent.
teaching: Use exactly as prescribed and expect possible gradual iris or lash changes; these cosmetic changes do not mean the drug is failing.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be performed within scope; acute eye pain or vision change requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving extra latanoprost doses because the pressure is high without a provider-directed change.
oneLinePearl: Latanoprost lowers pressure slowly; extra doses are not better.
sourceBasis: DailyMed Latanoprost Ophthalmic Solution labeling, updated 2026

title: Brimonidine: Pressure Lowering With Systemic Caution
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that lowers intraocular pressure. It can cause fatigue, dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension, and pediatric use has important product-specific restrictions because profound CNS depression can occur in very young children.
recognize: Fatigue, somnolence, dry mouth, or dizziness can occur despite topical administration.
Older adults taking antihypertensives may be more vulnerable to orthostasis and falls.
priorities: Assess dizziness, sedation, BP concerns, and fall risk.
Use punctal occlusion when instructed to reduce systemic absorption.
Verify age-specific appropriateness rather than assuming all eye drops are safe for children.
assessMonitor: Trend BP symptoms, sedation, falls, eye irritation, and IOP follow-up.
interventions: Teach slow position changes when dizziness occurs and use clean drop technique.
medicationSafety: Concomitant CNS depressants or antihypertensives can intensify sedation or hypotension.
Pediatric restrictions are product-specific and must be checked before administration.
teaching: Report fainting, severe drowsiness, or breathing problems and use only for the person and eye prescribed.
delegationScope: Medication administration follows scope; severe sedation or hypotension requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming topical brimonidine cannot contribute to dizziness or hypotension.
oneLinePearl: Topical alpha-2 therapy can still lower the whole patient, not just eye pressure.

title: Dorzolamide: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor Eye Drops
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Dorzolamide lowers intraocular pressure by reducing aqueous-humor production. Local burning and bitter taste are common, but severe renal impairment, significant sulfonamide-type reactions, or major ocular irritation require closer review.
recognize: Transient stinging, blurred vision, or bitter taste can occur after instillation.
Because dorzolamide is systemically absorbed, clinically important sulfonamide-type reactions are possible even with topical use.
priorities: Verify renal history and allergy history when clinically relevant.
Use clean drop technique and punctal occlusion when instructed.
Report severe rash, swelling, breathing difficulty, or marked ocular inflammation.
assessMonitor: Monitor eye comfort, adherence, renal-risk context, allergic symptoms, and IOP follow-up.
interventions: Separate other eye drops by the prescribed interval and avoid touching the tip to the eye.
medicationSafety: Do not treat a prior severe sulfonamide reaction as irrelevant simply because dorzolamide is an eye drop.
Use in severe renal impairment requires product-specific clinical review.
teaching: A brief bitter taste can occur; severe rash, swelling, or breathing difficulty is not routine and needs urgent attention.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; severe allergic or ocular symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Ignoring systemic allergy history because the medication is topical.
oneLinePearl: Dorzolamide is topical, but systemic sulfonamide-type safety still matters.

title: Pilocarpine: Miosis and Visual Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist that causes miosis and can lower intraocular pressure in selected conditions. Dim vision, accommodative spasm, and brow ache can occur; sudden flashes, floaters, or curtain-like vision require urgent evaluation for retinal complications.
recognize: Night vision can worsen because the pupil constricts.
Headache or brow ache may occur after dosing, especially early in therapy.
priorities: Assess ability to ambulate safely in dim light.
Teach clean drop technique and punctal occlusion when instructed.
Escalate sudden flashes, floaters, or major visual-field loss.
assessMonitor: Monitor visual function, falls, headache/brow pain, and ophthalmology follow-up.
interventions: Improve lighting and fall precautions when miosis impairs vision.
medicationSafety: Patients at risk for retinal detachment need ophthalmic evaluation according to the treatment plan.
Do not drive or perform hazardous tasks if vision is impaired after dosing.
teaching: Expect smaller pupils and possible dim vision; report sudden flashes, floaters, or a curtain over vision immediately.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within scope; acute visual symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient that new flashes and floaters are just expected miosis.
oneLinePearl: Pilocarpine makes the pupil small; sudden retinal symptoms are not normal.

title: Rho(D) Immune Globulin: Prevent Sensitization
bottomLine: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents Rh sensitization in an unsensitized Rh-negative patient after routine antepartum prophylaxis and selected sensitizing events. Postpartum doses are given to the mother when indicated—not to the newborn—and product route/dose depend on the specific preparation and fetomaternal exposure.
recognize: Common triggers include routine late-pregnancy prophylaxis, delivery of an Rh-positive/unknown-status infant, pregnancy loss, ectopic pregnancy, abdominal trauma, or invasive obstetric procedures.
The drug prevents sensitization; it does not remove antibodies once true alloimmunization has already occurred.
priorities: Verify maternal Rh status, antibody-screen context, event, infant Rh status when relevant, and the exact product/order.
Administer within the prescribed event-specific window.
For large fetomaternal hemorrhage, additional dosing may be required based on testing.
assessMonitor: Monitor for injection reaction, hypersensitivity, and completion of indicated fetomaternal hemorrhage testing.
interventions: Document product, lot, route, site, and indication according to policy.
medicationSafety: Postpartum Rho(D) immune globulin is maternal medication; do not inject the newborn.
Do not confuse micrograms with international units when interpreting product labeling.
complications: Maternal sensitization if prophylaxis is missed or inadequate
redFlags: Evidence of significant fetomaternal hemorrhage without adequate dose assessment
teaching: Explain that the medication protects future pregnancies by preventing the immune system from forming anti-D antibodies.
delegationScope: Verification of indication and maternal/infant blood-group data is a licensed-nurse responsibility; administration follows state/facility scope.
examTrap: Giving the postpartum Rho(D) immune globulin dose to the newborn instead of the mother.
oneLinePearl: RhIG prevents sensitization; it does not treat established alloimmunization.

title: Antenatal Betamethasone: Fetal Maturation, Not Tocolysis
bottomLine: Antenatal corticosteroids are given when preterm birth risk is high to accelerate fetal organ maturation; they do not stop labor. Timing depends on gestational age and likelihood of delivery, and maternal glucose can rise transiently after treatment.
recognize: Patients with diabetes may require closer glucose monitoring after corticosteroid administration.
A medically indicated delivery should not be delayed solely to complete the steroid course when maternal or fetal condition requires delivery.
priorities: Verify gestational age, estimated delivery risk, prior steroid course, and obstetric plan.
Monitor glucose closely in patients with diabetes or hyperglycemia risk.
Continue evaluation of the underlying preterm-birth trigger.
assessMonitor: Trend maternal glucose, infection/PPROM context, fetal status as ordered, and timing of doses.
interventions: Administer the prescribed course and coordinate neonatal/obstetric planning.
medicationSafety: Serial repeat courses are not routine.
Do not confuse fetal-maturation corticosteroids with medications used to suppress contractions.
complications: Inappropriate delay of necessary delivery if therapy is misunderstood
teaching: Explain that the goal is to improve fetal readiness for preterm birth, not to guarantee that labor will stop.
delegationScope: Gestational eligibility and obstetric decision-making require licensed obstetric evaluation; administration follows scope/policy.
examTrap: Telling the patient betamethasone is being given to stop contractions.
oneLinePearl: Betamethasone matures the fetus; it does not arrest labor.
sourceBasis: ACOG Antenatal Corticosteroid Therapy for Fetal Maturation
ACOG Preterm Labor and Birth guidance

title: Terbutaline in Obstetrics: Short-Term, Monitored Use
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Terbutaline may be used in selected monitored obstetric situations, but prolonged treatment for preterm labor is unsafe. Maternal tachycardia, arrhythmia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, chest pain, or pulmonary edema require prompt reassessment.
recognize: Expected beta-agonist effects include tremor and tachycardia.
Serious maternal cardiovascular events become more concerning with prolonged or excessive exposure.
priorities: Assess pulse, BP, respiratory status, chest symptoms, glucose, and potassium when indicated.
Follow strict duration and indication limits.
Stop/escalate for severe chest pain, dyspnea, arrhythmia, or pulmonary edema signs according to protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend maternal HR, BP, respiratory symptoms, glucose, potassium, contraction pattern, and fetal status as ordered.
interventions: Use only within an obstetric plan and monitored setting when indicated.
medicationSafety: Oral terbutaline should not be used for treatment or prevention of preterm labor.
Prolonged injectable therapy for preterm labor is not appropriate.
teaching: Report chest pain, shortness of breath, or a racing/irregular heartbeat immediately.
delegationScope: Use and monitoring are facility- and role-specific; maternal instability requires immediate licensed obstetric escalation.
examTrap: Treating terbutaline as a routine long-term outpatient medication for preterm-labor prevention.
oneLinePearl: Terbutaline may buy time briefly; it is not a long-term tocolysis plan.
sourceBasis: FDA terbutaline boxed-warning safety communication and labeling

title: Nifedipine for Tocolysis: Watch the Pressure
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Nifedipine may be used off-label for short-term tocolysis in selected pregnancies. Its major nursing safety issue is maternal hypotension; treatment remains a time-limited strategy to support fetal-benefit interventions, not a cure for the cause of preterm labor.
recognize: Headache, flushing, dizziness, and hypotension may occur.
Patients with low baseline BP or hemodynamic instability may not tolerate therapy.
priorities: Check maternal BP and symptoms before and during therapy according to protocol.
Assess contractions, fetal status, and the reason preterm birth is threatened.
Escalate symptomatic hypotension or fetal deterioration.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, pulse, dizziness, contraction pattern, and fetal status as ordered.
interventions: Use fall precautions for dizziness and support maternal positioning/perfusion according to the obstetric plan.
medicationSafety: Tocolysis is inappropriate when delivery is required for major maternal/fetal compromise, severe bleeding, or infection.
Do not extrapolate chronic hypertension dosing into a tocolysis regimen.
complications: Reduced uteroplacental perfusion if hypotension is severe
teaching: Explain that the medication is intended to delay delivery briefly when clinically appropriate, not to guarantee continuation of pregnancy.
delegationScope: Tocolytic administration/monitoring authority varies by state and setting; abnormal maternal or fetal findings require licensed obstetric assessment.
examTrap: Continuing nifedipine despite symptomatic hypotension because contractions have slowed.
oneLinePearl: Tocolysis only helps if maternal perfusion stays safe.
sourceBasis: ACOG Preterm Labor and Birth guidance

title: Methylergonovine: Uterine Tone With Hypertension Risk
bottomLine: Methylergonovine increases uterine tone and may be used for postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony, but its vasoconstrictive effect can cause severe hypertension. Avoid or question use in hypertension or preeclampsia according to protocol.
recognize: A boggy uterus with postpartum bleeding may prompt uterotonic therapy.
Severe headache, chest pain, or markedly elevated BP after administration is concerning for excessive vasoconstriction/hypertensive toxicity.
priorities: Check BP and hypertensive-disorder history before administration.
Assess uterine tone and bleeding response.
Escalate severe hypertension, chest pain, neurologic symptoms, or persistent hemorrhage.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, pulse, uterine tone, quantified blood loss, headache, chest symptoms, and perfusion.
interventions: Use within the postpartum hemorrhage pathway and reassess whether another cause such as trauma or retained tissue is driving bleeding.
medicationSafety: Methylergonovine is generally avoided in hypertension/preeclampsia.
Do not let a uterotonic choice delay activation of the hemorrhage protocol in unstable bleeding.
teaching: Report severe headache, chest pain, or shortness of breath immediately.
delegationScope: Uterotonic administration and hemorrhage assessment follow obstetric competency and state/facility scope.
examTrap: Giving methylergonovine to a patient with severe preeclampsia without questioning the order.
oneLinePearl: Methylergonovine squeezes the uterus—and can squeeze the vessels too hard.
